newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ciampi says Italy to be in EMU from the start.
newsitem.headline: Ciampi says Italy to be in EMU from the start.

text.p: Italy's Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi reaffirmed on Friday Italy's commitment to be in the EMU from its start and as an element of stability, "not of distortion".
Speaking at the European Banking Congress in Frankfurt, Ciampi said: "Italy intends to be one of the founding members of the EMU".
He added: "Italians are determined to do everything necessary to be an element of stability and not an element of tension or distortion".
Ciampi said inflation was now under control, noting that "in November it had fallen to 2.6 percent, according to preliminary data".
He added that the government target for 1997 of an average 2.5 percent inflation rate was "within reach".
The lira has been stable for many months at an average level of just 1,000 lire to the deutschemark, he noted.
This, coupled with lower interest rates, reflected the widespread conviction that Italy will be eligible to join the single currency in 1999, he said.
Ciampi says Italy to be in EMU from the start=3
Ciampi rejected criticism about the one-off 12.5 trillion lire "tax for Europe" that Italians will face in 1997 to meet the 3.0 percent deficit-to-GDP Maastricht criterion.
He explained it was one-off measure aimed at bringing forward by one year the 1998 goal Italy had already set itself to reach the criterion.
"This does not relieve government from its commitment to tough measures to bring the deficit below three percent in 1998," he said.
The task of containing the deficit under that level in the following years "is not just credible but actually easier to achieve", given Italy's growing primary surplus, he said.
Ciampi also reaffirmed that "Italy is wholly in favour of any measure, including the stability pact, to guarantee a strong Euro, not only out of conviction but also convenience".
Stressing that only a unified Europe, where Italy can play a central role, would be able to face future world challenges, Ciampi concluded that "Italy needs Europe, but Europe also needs Italy".
